description_ru: Неделя в поезде от Москвы до Владивостока: проводница с самоваром, берёзовые горизонты и Байкал, который заставляет замолчать даже самых болтливых пассажиров.
text:
The Trans-Siberian railway is not so much a journey as a prolonged conversation with distance, conducted at the speed of a bicycle on a downhill road and punctuated by sudden outbreaks of boiled potatoes. It runs from Moscow to Vladivostok, a little over nine thousand kilometres of track, across seven time zones, and the timetable, to avoid confusing everybody, is written entirely in Moscow time. One quickly learns that the clock in the corridor has little to do with the sun outside the window, and after the third day, one stops caring, which is the first sign of recovery from modern life.

Mine was a second-class compartment, which is to say a small cell with four bunks, a folding table and a window, shared with three strangers who by the end of the week had become, in the manner of such places, either cherished friends or subjects of fascinated resentment. The car was commanded by a provodnitsa, a formidable woman in a blue uniform and a bouffant of unnatural permanence, who held the keys, the samovar, and the moral authority of a ship's captain. She inspected my ticket as though it were a forgery by a minor genius, then handed me a set of sheets and said, in the tone of a judge passing a light sentence, "Tea at six."

The tea, I soon discovered, was the organising principle of the day. At the end of the carriage the great metal samovar bubbled with water that was always hot, and from morning until night, passengers drifted down the corridor in slippers and tracksuits, clutching glasses in ornate metal holders, like a procession of pilgrims in search of an unusually mundane relic. To these glasses we added instant noodles, sachets of coffee, and, as the days wore on, an unspoken but unmistakable ceremony of sharing. A grandmother produced pies from a bag the size of a suitcase. A young soldier, shy as a deer, offered smoked fish. Somebody always had a deck of cards, and somebody else always cheated.

Outside, Russia unrolled, and it unrolled in an extraordinary monotony that turned, after several hours, into a kind of grandeur. For a day and a half there were birches: white-barked, slender, standing in the pale sunlight like an audience of ghosts that had come to see the train off, and which, having done so, simply went on standing there. Then came the Urals, which are not so much mountains as a long, polite undulation of the earth, and a modest obelisk at the border announcing that we had passed from Europe into Asia. I looked out of the window for some sign of the transformation. The birches continued unaltered.

Cities arrived like islands in a green ocean, each with a platform, a vendor on it selling dried fish and pickled cucumbers from a bucket, and a stop of precisely twenty minutes, long enough to buy a loaf of bread and not long enough to lose the train, although a surprising number of people attempt to do both. At Novosibirsk, the largest city of Siberia, a man with a gold tooth sold me a jar of honey and a short, passionate lecture on the superiority of mountain bees. In the middle of the night, at some unnamed halt, I heard the long, hollow knocking of a mallet on iron, as an inspector tapped each wheel to check for flaws. It is a sound that follows you into your dreams and lingers there, the heartbeat of a very large animal.

On the fifth day, the landscape began to tilt, and the conversation of the carriage dropped. The line curled around the southern tip of Lake Baikal, and then, for hours, followed its shore, with the lake on one side of the train and wooded hills on the other, and nobody in the compartment said a word. Baikal is not a lake in any ordinary sense. It is the deepest on Earth, at about 1,640 metres, and it is some twenty-five million years old, which makes it the oldest too. It holds roughly a fifth of all the unfrozen fresh water on the surface of the planet, more than all the North American Great Lakes combined, and the water is so clear that a diver may see objects at a depth of forty metres. The surface that morning was a pane of pewter, and a thin mist hung above it like a thought that nobody had finished.

I got off at Irkutsk, and took a rattling minibus to the village of Listvyanka, where I ate omul, the lake's famous silvery fish, smoked until it fell off the bone, on a wooden bench with a babushka who sold it from a stall. She watched me eat the first piece with an anxious intensity that suggested my reaction would be reported to higher authorities. I said that it was the best fish I had ever eaten, and I was telling the truth, which seemed to satisfy her; she gave me a second portion and a gruff, approving nod.

Later, walking along the shore, I came across a stretch of ice that had begun to form in the shallows even in early autumn, and I stood and listened as it creaked and sang, a strange, eerie music, like a whale being rehearsed by a cathedral organ. In winter, Baikal freezes so solidly that trucks drive across it, and the ice is clear as glass, with great cracks that run like lightning beneath your feet. I have rarely felt so small, or been so contented about it.

The train resumed its progress, and over the last two days the landscape slid into the east, into a country of hills and rivers and rusting bridges, until the Pacific appeared, grey and indifferent, at the end of the line. Vladivostok received us with fog. I climbed down onto the platform with a stiff back, a bag of stale pies, and the curious sensation that I had been rocked in a cradle for a week, and was not sure I wished to be woken. The provodnitsa saluted me from the carriage step, with the gravity of a woman who has seen ten thousand passengers off and expects, with weary optimism, a thousand more.

"You were not so much trouble," she said, and it was the nicest thing anyone said to me the whole year.

questions.question: How long is the Trans-Siberian route?
questions.answer: A little over nine thousand kilometres, from Moscow to Vladivostok.

questions.question: What does the provodnitsa control?
questions.answer: The carriage: tickets, sheets, the samovar and discipline.

questions.question: What is special about Lake Baikal?
questions.answer: It is the deepest and oldest lake on Earth and holds a fifth of surface fresh water.
